query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing TOR-TILD’s EAM reference with a machine-learning (ML) interatomic potential trained on ab initio data for high-entropy alloy liquids and solids near their melting points will substantially improve the overlap between reference-model and ab initio configuration spaces, reducing the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to EAM.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures
generation.intervention: Develop and use a machine-learning interatomic potential—trained via active learning on ab initio force and energy data spanning relevant high-temperature configurations—as the reference in place of classical EAM potentials
generation.conditions: Focus on representative quinary or higher-component compositions in a temperature window from ~0.8Tm to 1.1Tm, encompassing both solid and liquid regimes
generation.structural_mediator: Expanded local-environment coverage in the ML potential, capturing broad configurational disorder in the high-entropy alloy liquid and near-melting solid
generation.mechanism: The ML reference more faithfully mimics ab initio energetics and forces, improving the overlap between the reference and target phase spaces in thermodynamic integration and thereby mitigating path-length-driven errors observed with EAM references
generation.predicted_outcome: Free-energy differences relative to ab initio will be systematically smaller than those seen with EAM-based TOR-TILD, for example, by reducing path-integration errors by tens of meV/atom or more
generation.baseline: Previous TOR-TILD calculations relying on EAM references, which exhibit large path mismatches for high-temperature liquid configurations
generation.boundary: Most effective for 5+ component alloys with significant atomic-size mismatch at high temperatures, though performance might degrade for extremely wide composition ranges or extremely high melting points
generation.uncertainty: Less established for highly complex element combinations beyond select quinary or senary sets. Requires extensive high-temperature ab initio training data for robust ML potential fidelity

falsification_experiment.design: Compute MELT or integrate from a known reference to ab initio using the ML potential, then compare thermodynamic observables (e.g., Helmholtz free energies) for high-temperature solid and liquid states directly with fully ab initio integration in small cells.
measurements: Ab initio energies and forces to train the ML potential over a range of relevant disordered configurations
Thermodynamic integration paths (e.g., λ-coupling) for ML→ab initio and EAM→ab initio references
Converged free energies of melting or chemical potentials in the liquid from both the ML-based and EAM-based references, each compared to direct ab initio results
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-based reference fails to reduce the integration path mismatch below the typical EAM-based level (for example, if the free-energy discrepancy relative to ab initio exceeds that of TOR-TILD’s EAM references at Tm), the hypothesis is falsified.

[ [1] ] Although many physical and chemical fabrication methods have been developed [ [2] ] there are still many gray areas concerning the synthesis‐structure‐properties relationships in these complex nanomaterials. The synergy of several effects makes HENA potentially efficient and stable nano‐catalysts: the “cocktail” effect due to the interaction between the different elements can give rise to enhanced reactivity which counterbalances the low content of noble metals in the nanostructure. The variety of elements and atomic sizes generate many lattice distortions and crystalline defects that can create preferential surface reaction sites. Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. decision.trend: Both PMC11375216 and PMC11775865 employed classical embedded-atom-method (EAM) potentials to study multicomponent high-entropy alloys (HfNbTaTiZr and AuCoCuNiPt) at elevated temperatures. In PMC11375216, non-equilibrium molecular dynamics with an EAM potential was able to capture short-range order (SRO) effects on phonon conduction at 300 K but did not address the liquid regime at high temperatures. In contrast, PMC11775865 extended EAM-based MD simulations up to 1500 K, uncovering phase separation and coalescence phenomena in high-entropy nanoalloys. However, both studies highlighted difficulties in fully representing the complex configuration space—particularly in the liquid or near-melting regime—and indicated that classical potentials struggle to match ab initio accuracy when sampling the broad range of local atomic motifs. This leaves open the challenge of bridging the gap between efficient classical references (EAM) and more accurate, but computationally demanding, ab initio calculations for high-entropy alloy liquids near their melting points.
decision.unsolved: Despite partial success modeling high-entropy alloys at moderate to high temperatures, the existing EAM references do not sufficiently cover the vast array of instantaneous local atomic configurations in the high-temperature liquid state. A key challenge remains improving phase-space overlap so that thermodynamic-integration schemes (e.g., TOR-TILD) do not suffer large path mismatches when moving between classical and ab initio descriptions of these alloys near their melting temperatures.
decision.lever: Train a machine-learning interatomic potential (e.g., based on local environment descriptors) against dense ab initio data sampled from the high-entropy alloy liquid and solid near the melting point, using active-learning cycles to ensure coverage of the relevant high-temperature configuration space. Apply thermodynamic integration that uses this ML potential as the reference for the ab initio target, focusing on an extended temperature range (e.g., 0.8–1.1 Tm) and representative compositions with carefully selected training data for disordered states.
decision.why: ML potentials, when trained on a comprehensive set of liquid and solid configurations generated via ab initio calculations, can more accurately capture the diverse local coordination environments that classical EAM fails to reproduce. This improved reference–target overlap will reduce the path mismatch in thermodynamic integration (relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM), because the reference potential will more faithfully mimic the target energy landscape. Existing demonstrations in simpler systems (e.g., binary and ternary alloys at high temperatures) have shown that ML-based potentials can provide quantum-accurate energies and forces with lower computational cost than pure ab initio methods. A conclusive free-energy benchmark would compare the predicted melting free energies (or other thermodynamic observables, such as chemical potentials in the liquid) from the ML-refined integration path directly to fully ab initio calculations in small supercells, determining consistency within a tight numeric tolerance (e.g., ±1 meV/atom) to validate or disprove the approach.
